description: We're a six person team building a clearer way to see fire from space. Satellite fire monitoring is one of NASA's most valuable data streams, yet MODIS and VIIRS still tell their stories at different resolutions, which makes long term comparison hard. Our team brings together a data analyst, a researcher, a science strategist, a web developer, a video editor, and a team leader to turn open NASA FIRMS data into one consistent, easy to explore picture, so anyone can spot unusual fire activity.
summary: Ember Grid is a web platform that ingests NASA FIRMS active fire records from MODIS and VIIRS and turns them into one consistent, explorable history of fire activity. Comparing the two sensors directly is hard because they differ in resolution and observation patterns, so most tools leave users to reconcile the gaps themselves. We built a full end to end pipeline instead: cleaning the records to remove volcanoes, industrial flares, and low confidence detections, mapping both sensors onto a shared 1 km daily grid using location and Fire Radiative Power, calculating multi year monthly medians, and flagging fire anomalies against them. Results are delivered through an interactive dashboard where users pick an area, date range, and satellite and switch between Raw and Harmonized views, alongside a fire calendar, alerts, risk analytics, email subscriptions, and downloadable GeoJSON, CSV, and reports. A Methods & Provenance page documents every step, and we state clearly that hotspots are observations, not confirmed wildfire boundaries. This matters because fire response and research depend on data people can trust. By harmonizing two satellite records and keeping the raw data one click away, Ember Grid helps researchers, analysts, and communities spot unusual fire activity sooner and understand what the data does and doesn’t show.
details:
Ember Grid is a full stack web application that combines NASA satellite data, a custom harmonization pipeline, and interactive exploration tools to make fire activity easier to understand. The system ingests historical MODIS and VIIRS active fire records from NASA FIRMS data, cleans them by removing volcanoes, industrial flares, and low confidence detections, and maps both sensors onto a shared 1 km daily grid using location and Fire Radiative Power. From that unified record, it calculates multi year monthly medians and flags fire anomalies against them. Users can choose an Area of Interest, date range, and satellite, then switch between Raw and Harmonized views to see exactly what the processing changed. The platform also includes a fire calendar, alerts, risk analytics, email subscriptions, and downloadable GeoJSON, CSV, and reports.

The benefits are consistency and trust. MODIS and VIIRS differ in resolution and observation patterns, so comparing their raw hotspots directly can mislead. By harmonizing the two and keeping the original observations one click away, Ember Grid gives researchers, analysts, and communities a clear way to spot unusual fire activity and study long term patterns at their area of interst. The intended impact is a dependable, accessible tool that turns two complicated satellite records into one picture people can actually use.

We built the project with Python (NumPy, Pandas) for data processing and Next.js, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS for the web application. The data comes from NASA FIRMS, and the live platform is deployed at vercel. We used Super Intelligence (SI) tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Google Antigravity, and GitHub Copilot to assist with planning, development, research, image generation, content enhancement and documentation, and the team reviewed and takes responsibility for the final work.

The project is creative because it treats harmonization as something users can see and question, not a hidden step. The Raw and Harmonized toggle lets anyone compare the source data with the processed result, and a Methods & Provenance page documents the sources, workflow, and assumptions behind it. We also state plainly that satellite hotspots are observations, not confirmed wildfire boundaries or verified emergencies. We designed for both scientific care and usability, delivering not just code but a dashboard, alerts, exportable data, and a clear workflow that makes complex satellite science accessible.

The Project GitHub Repository Link: https://github.com/shakhawat2021hossain/ember-grid
